units.title: Hypertensive Disorders: Classification & Definitions
units.guide: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are classified into four main entities: Chronic Hypertension (predating conception or before 20 weeks), Gestational Hypertension (onset after 20 weeks without proteinuria), Pre-eclampsia (new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction), and Chronic Hypertension with Superimposed Pre-eclampsia.

units.title: Pathophysiology: Trophoblast Invasion & Angiogenic Imbalance
units.guide: Failed second wave of endovascular trophoblast invasion at 16-18 weeks leaves high-resistance muscular spiral arteries. Placental ischemia triggers shedding of anti-angiogenic factors (soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 [sFlt-1] and soluble endoglin [sEng]), which neutralize pro-angiogenic PlGF and VEGF, causing widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction.

units.title: Predictive Screening: Uterine Doppler, Biomarkers & Aspirin Prophylaxis
units.guide: Persistent bilateral early diastolic notch and elevated pulsatility index on uterine artery Doppler at 20-24 weeks indicate impaired trophoblast remodeling. Low-dose aspirin (150 mg nightly initiated before 16 weeks) significantly reduces preterm pre-eclampsia by restoring the prostacyclin-thromboxane balance in high-risk women.

units.title: Pre-eclampsia: Severe Features & Laboratory Criteria
units.guide: Severe features include systolic BP >=160 mmHg or diastolic >=110 mmHg, platelets <100,000/microL, serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL (or doubling), transaminases elevated 2x normal, pulmonary edema, or new-onset visual/cerebral disturbances. Note that massive proteinuria alone (>5 g/24h) is no longer classified as a severe feature under current ACOG criteria.

units.title: Acute Antihypertensive Therapy & Hemodynamic Targets
units.guide: Severe acute hypertension (BP >=160/110 mmHg sustained for 15 minutes) requires immediate urgent lowering within 30-60 minutes using IV labetalol, oral immediate-release nifedipine, or IV hydralazine. Blood pressure should be titrated to 130-150 / 80-100 mmHg; ACE inhibitors and ARBs are strictly contraindicated due to fetal fetopathy.

units.title: Eclampsia: Stages, Convulsions & Resuscitation
units.guide: Eclampsia is the occurrence of generalized tonic-clonic convulsions or coma in a pre-eclamptic patient. Seizure evolves through four classic phases: premonitory stage, tonic stage, clonic stage, and comatose stage. Emergency management prioritizes airway, breathing, left lateral positioning, and seizure arrest with magnesium sulfate; delivery is delayed until the mother is stabilized.

units.title: Magnesium Sulfate Protocols & Toxicity Monitoring
units.guide: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis and treatment (Pritchard IM or Zuspan IV regimen). Therapeutic serum magnesium range is 4 to 7 mEq/L (4.8 to 8.4 mg/dL). Clinical monitoring requires verifying present deep tendon (patellar) reflexes, respiratory rate >=12/min, and urine output >=30 mL/h (or 100 mL/4h); toxicity is reversed with 10% calcium gluconate IV.

units.title: HELLP Syndrome & Delivery Timing Strategies
units.guide: HELLP syndrome consists of Hemolysis (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes), Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets (<100,000/microL). Definitive treatment is delivery: at 37 weeks for gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia without severe features; at 34 weeks for pre-eclampsia with severe features; or immediate delivery regardless of gestational age upon eclampsia, pulmonary edema, or HELLP syndrome.

questions.q: What diagnostic criterion defines hypertension in pregnancy on clinical examination?
opts: Systolic blood pressure >= 140 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure >= 90 mmHg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart
Systolic BP >= 130 mmHg on a single random reading
Diastolic BP >= 80 mmHg on continuous ambulatory monitoring
Mean arterial pressure >= 85 mmHg at 12 weeks
questions.exp: Hypertension is defined as systolic BP >= 140 mmHg and/or diastolic BP >= 90 mmHg on two readings taken >= 4 hours apart. (Book p391)

questions.q: Which Korotkoff sound phase is the gold standard for recording maternal diastolic blood pressure during pregnancy?
opts: Korotkoff phase V (complete disappearance of sound)
questions.exp: ACOG and international guidelines specify Korotkoff phase V (disappearance of sounds) as the definitive measure of diastolic blood pressure in pregnancy. (Book p391)

questions.q: How is Gestational Hypertension defined according to international criteria?
opts: New-onset hypertension developing after 20 weeks of gestation without significant proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction
Hypertension developing after 20 weeks accompanied by 3+ proteinuria
Transient blood pressure elevation during labor only
questions.exp: Gestational hypertension is new-onset BP >= 140/90 mmHg appearing after 20 weeks of gestation in the absence of proteinuria or systemic end-organ signs. (Book p391)

questions.q: What is the standard quantitative 24-hour urine collection cutoff for defining significant proteinuria in pre-eclampsia?
opts: >= 300 mg of protein in a 24-hour urine collection (or spot urine protein:creatinine ratio >= 0.3 mg/mg)
questions.exp: Proteinuria is defined as >= 300 mg/24h urine protein, or a urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) >= 0.3 mg/mg. (Book p392)

questions.q: Can a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia be established in the ABSENCE of proteinuria?
opts: Yes, if new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks is accompanied by any severe feature (e.g., thrombocytopenia, renal insufficiency, impaired liver function, pulmonary edema)
No, proteinuria is mandatory under all definitions
Only if twin pregnancy is confirmed
Only if serum albumin is <1.0 g/dL
questions.exp: Under revised criteria, pre-eclampsia can be diagnosed without proteinuria if new hypertension is accompanied by thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, renal failure, or pulmonary edema. (Book p392)

questions.q: What abnormal physiological event in early placentation initiates the pathogenesis of pre-eclampsia?
opts: Failure of the second wave of endovascular trophoblast invasion of the spiral arteries into the myometrium at 16 to 18 weeks
Excessive deep penetration of syncytiotrophoblasts into maternal pelvic veins
Early physiological calcification of the placenta
questions.exp: Defective secondary trophoblast invasion (16-18w) leaves spiral arteries narrow, muscular, and high-resistance, causing chronic placental hypoperfusion. (Book p396)

questions.q: Which circulating anti-angiogenic factor secreted by the ischemic placenta plays a central role in widespread maternal endothelial cell injury?
questions.exp: sFlt-1 acts as a circulating decoy receptor that binds and neutralizes pro-angiogenic VEGF and PlGF, precipitating maternal systemic endothelial dysfunction. (Book p396)

questions.q: What characteristic renal histological lesion is pathognomonic for pre-eclampsia on renal biopsy?
opts: Glomerular capillary endotheliosis (swollen endothelial cells encroaching on the capillary lumina)
questions.exp: Glomerular capillary endotheliosis, marked by endothelial swelling and subendothelial fibrinoid deposition, is the classic histological hallmark of pre-eclampsia. (Book p396)

questions.q: Why does maternal blood volume exhibit a paradoxical state in severe pre-eclampsia?
opts: Intravascular volume is contracted due to diffuse capillary leakage into the interstitial space despite total body edema
Intravascular blood volume is massively expanded by 100%
The patient experiences profound polycythemia and hypervolemia
Plasma oncotic pressure is markedly elevated
questions.exp: Endothelial breakdown allows albumin and fluid to leak into the interstitium, causing generalized edema alongside significant intravascular hypovolemia. (Book p397)

questions.q: What abnormal uterine artery Doppler finding at 20 to 24 weeks of gestation predicts an increased risk for early-onset pre-eclampsia?
opts: Persistence of bilateral early diastolic notching and an elevated pulsatility index (PI)
Reversal of end-diastolic flow in the ductus venosus
Increased systolic flow velocity without notching
questions.exp: Persistence of the early diastolic notch beyond 20-24 weeks indicates high resistance in the uteroplacental bed due to failure of spiral artery remodeling. (Book p397)

questions.q: What clinical value does an sFlt-1 to PlGF ratio < 38 have in women presenting with suspected pre-eclampsia between 24 and 37 weeks?
opts: A high negative predictive value (>99%) to reliably rule out the development of pre-eclampsia for up to 1 to 4 weeks
Confirms an immediate requirement for Caesarean delivery within 2 hours
Diagnoses acute fatty liver of pregnancy
questions.exp: According to the PROGNOSIS trial, an sFlt-1:PlGF ratio < 38 safely rules out pre-eclampsia for up to 4 weeks, avoiding unnecessary hospital admissions. (Book p398)

questions.q: When should low-dose aspirin prophylaxis (150 mg nightly) be initiated in women identified as high risk for pre-eclampsia?
opts: Before 16 weeks of gestation (ideally between 11 and 14 weeks)
questions.exp: Initiating low-dose aspirin before 16 weeks (prior to completion of secondary trophoblast invasion) dramatically lowers the risk of preterm pre-eclampsia. (Book p398)

questions.q: What is the biochemical mechanism by which low-dose aspirin prevents pre-eclampsia?
opts: Selectively inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase (COX-1), restoring the balance between prostacyclin (vasodilator) and thromboxane A2 (vasoconstrictor)
Blocks renal sodium reabsorption like a loop diuretic
Directly binds and neutralizes placental sFlt-1
questions.exp: Low-dose aspirin preferentially inhibits thromboxane A2 (platelet aggregator/vasoconstrictor) while sparing endothelial prostacyclin (vasodilator). (Book p399)

questions.q: What dietary supplement is recommended by the WHO to prevent pre-eclampsia in populations with low dietary calcium intake?
opts: Elemental Calcium 1.5 to 2.0 g/day administered orally
questions.exp: Calcium supplementation (1.5-2.0 g/day) in calcium-deficient populations reduces the incidence of pre-eclampsia by modulating vascular smooth muscle reactivity. (Book p399)

questions.q: Which of the following blood pressure readings meets the criteria for pre-eclampsia with SEVERE features?
opts: Systolic BP >= 160 mmHg and/or Diastolic BP >= 110 mmHg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart while on bed rest
Systolic BP 140-150 mmHg on two occasions
Diastolic BP 90-100 mmHg on two occasions
Systolic BP 135 mmHg and diastolic BP 85 mmHg
questions.exp: Blood pressure >= 160 mmHg systolic or >= 110 mmHg diastolic is an unequivocal severe feature of pre-eclampsia. (Book p392)

questions.q: What platelet count threshold defines thrombocytopenia as a severe feature of pre-eclampsia?
questions.exp: Platelets < 100,000 / microL represents a severe feature indicating progressive consumption coagulopathy and microvascular damage. (Book p393)

questions.q: Which hepatic manifestation in pre-eclampsia is an ominous warning sign of imminent subcapsular liver hematoma rupture?
opts: Severe, persistent epigastric or right upper quadrant pain unresponsive to analgesics
questions.exp: Severe epigastric or right upper quadrant pain results from hepatic ischemia and stretching of Glisson's capsule, heralding hepatic hematoma rupture. (Book p393)

questions.q: Why was massive proteinuria (>5 g/24h) REMOVED from the diagnostic criteria for pre-eclampsia with severe features in modern guidelines?
opts: Proteinuria quantity does not correlate linearly with maternal or adverse perinatal outcomes
Proteinuria cannot be measured in pregnant women
Proteinuria occurs in 100% of healthy pregnancies
Dipstick reagents are no longer manufactured
questions.exp: ACOG and ISSHP eliminated the 5 g/24h threshold because clinical severity and adverse outcomes depend on organ perfusion, not isolated urinary protein levels. (Book p394)

questions.q: Within what timeframe must severe acute maternal hypertension (BP >= 160/110 mmHg) be treated in an emergency setting?
opts: Within 30 to 60 minutes of confirmation, to prevent maternal intracerebral hemorrhage
Only after delivery of the infant
questions.exp: Severe acute hypertension is an obstetric emergency requiring pharmacological intervention within 30-60 minutes to avert hemorrhagic stroke. (Book p399)

questions.q: What are the three first-line pharmacological agents recommended for acute emergency control of severe gestational hypertension?
opts: Intravenous Labetalol, Oral Immediate-Release Nifedipine, and Intravenous Hydralazine
questions.exp: IV labetalol, oral rapid-acting nifedipine capsules, and IV hydralazine are the primary first-line agents for acute severe hypertension. (Book p400)

questions.q: What is the recommended target blood pressure range when treating acute severe pre-eclampsia?
opts: Systolic 130 to 150 mmHg and Diastolic 80 to 100 mmHg
questions.exp: The goal is to lower BP to 130-150 / 80-100 mmHg; overzealous reduction (<110/70) precipitates acute placental hypoperfusion and fetal distress. (Book p400)

questions.q: Why are Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) Inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs) ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy?
opts: They induce fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, and neonatal anuric renal failure
questions.exp: ACE inhibitors cause severe fetopathy: renal tubular dysgenesis, oligohydramnios (Potter sequence), pulmonary hypoplasia, and cranial bone hypoplasia. (Book p400)

questions.q: In an asthmatic pregnant patient with acute severe hypertension, which first-line antihypertensive should be avoided in favor of oral nifedipine or hydralazine?
opts: Intravenous Labetalol (due to potential non-selective beta-blocker induced bronchospasm)
questions.exp: Labetalol has non-selective beta-blocking activity that can trigger life-threatening bronchospasm in active asthma or congestive heart failure. (Book p400)

questions.q: What defines eclampsia in a pregnant or postpartum woman?
opts: Occurrence of new-onset generalized tonic-clonic convulsions or unexplained coma in a woman with pre-eclampsia
A transient focal motor tic without loss of consciousness
A systolic blood pressure > 180 mmHg alone
questions.exp: Eclampsia is defined as the development of grand mal convulsions or unexplained coma in a patient with pre-eclampsia, excluding other neurological causes. (Book p393)

questions.q: What is the correct sequential order of the four clinical stages of an eclamptic seizure?
opts: Premonitory stage -> Tonic stage -> Clonic stage -> Stage of coma
Clonic stage -> Tonic stage -> Aura -> Recovery
Stage of coma -> Tonic stage -> Clonic stage -> Recovery
Aura -> Clonic stage -> Postictal hyperreflexia -> Coma
questions.exp: Eclamptic convulsion progresses through: (1) Premonitory stage (20-30s), (2) Tonic stage (30s), (3) Clonic stage (1-4 min), and (4) Stage of coma. (Book p393)

questions.q: During an active eclamptic seizure, what is the immediate priority for the attending obstetric team?
opts: Protect airway, place patient in left lateral position, administer oxygen, and prevent physical trauma while preparing IV magnesium sulfate
Perform an immediate bedside emergency Caesarean section on the bed
Restrain the extremities forcefully with leather straps
questions.exp: Airway maintenance, lateral tilt to prevent aspiration, supplemental oxygen, and seizure arrest with MgSO4 are paramount; delivery during seizure is contraindicated. (Book p394)

questions.q: At what time period do the majority of eclamptic seizures occur relative to delivery?
opts: Antepartum (approx. 50%), followed by intrapartum (approx. 25-30%) and early postpartum (approx. 20-25%)
During second stage of labor only
questions.exp: Most eclamptic convulsions occur antepartum (~50%), though up to a third occur intrapartum and 20-25% occur postpartum (mostly within 48 hours). (Book p394)

questions.q: What is the primary drug of choice for the prevention and treatment of eclamptic convulsions?
questions.exp: The landmark Collaborative Eclampsia Trial established that magnesium sulfate is vastly superior to phenytoin and diazepam for preventing recurrent seizures. (Book p401)

questions.q: In the Pritchard intramuscular regimen for eclampsia, what is the loading dose administered?
opts: 4 g IV (20% solution over 5-10 min) PLUS 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock as 50% solution)
questions.exp: Pritchard loading dose: 4 g IV (20% solution) slowly plus 10 g IM (5 g of 50% solution deeply in each upper outer quadrant of the buttock). (Book p401)

questions.q: In the Zuspan intravenous regimen, what is the standard maintenance dose of magnesium sulfate?
opts: 1 to 2 g/hour by continuous intravenous infusion pump
questions.exp: Zuspan regimen: 4 g IV loading dose over 15-20 min followed by continuous IV maintenance infusion of 1 to 2 g/hour for 24 hours. (Book p401)

questions.q: What is the therapeutic target serum level of magnesium for preventing eclamptic seizures?
questions.exp: Therapeutic anti-convulsant serum range is 4 to 7 mEq/L (4.8 - 8.4 mg/dL or 2.0 - 3.5 mmol/L). (Book p402)

questions.q: What is the EARLIEST clinical sign of magnesium sulfate toxicity?
opts: Loss of deep tendon reflexes (patellar knee-jerk reflex disappears at 8-10 mEq/L)
questions.exp: Loss of the patellar knee-jerk reflex occurs at serum levels of 8-10 mEq/L and precedes life-threatening respiratory depression (>12 mEq/L). (Book p402)

questions.q: If a patient on magnesium sulfate exhibits loss of patellar reflexes and a respiratory rate of 8 breaths/min, what is the immediate antidote?
opts: 10 mL of 10% Calcium Gluconate IV administered slowly over 10 minutes
questions.exp: 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate (1 g) given IV over 10 minutes is the specific antidote that directly antagonizes magnesium toxicity. (Book p402)

questions.q: What does the clinical acronym HELLP syndrome stand for?
opts: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count
questions.exp: HELLP denotes microangiopathic Hemolysis (MAHA), Elevated Liver enzymes (transaminases), and Low Platelets (<100,000/microL). (Book p403)

questions.q: What peripheral blood smear finding confirms microangiopathic hemolysis in HELLP syndrome?
opts: Schistocytes (fragmented red blood cells / helmet cells) and burr cells
questions.exp: RBC fragmentation through damaged, fibrin-deposited microvasculature creates classic schistocytes, helmet cells, and elevated serum LDH. (Book p403)

questions.q: What is the definitive cure for pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and HELLP syndrome?
opts: Delivery of the fetus and complete removal of the placenta
questions.exp: Placenta is the pathogenic driver; delivery of the placenta halts release of anti-angiogenic factors and resolves the endothelial cascade. (Book p404)

questions.q: In a pregnant woman with Pre-eclampsia WITHOUT severe features at 37 weeks of gestation, what is the recommended management?
opts: Delivery (induction of labor or Caesarean as indicated)
questions.exp: At >=37 weeks (term), pre-eclampsia without severe features should be delivered because maternal/fetal risks outweigh benefits of continuation. (Book p404)

questions.q: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks of gestation is diagnosed with pre-eclampsia with severe features complicated by acute pulmonary edema and platelet count of 35,000/microL. What is the appropriate delivery timing?
opts: Immediate stabilization and delivery regardless of gestational age
Expectant management for at least 4 more weeks
Wait until 37 weeks to ensure mature fetal size
questions.exp: Life-threatening maternal complications (pulmonary edema, HELLP, eclampsia, renal failure) require immediate delivery once stabilized, regardless of GA. (Book p405)
